before: Before you practice, here's a quick summary of primes and factors. Everything important, in a few minutes.

before.say: A prime has exactly two divisors, one and itself. One is not prime, and neither are zero and the negative numbers. Two is prime, and it's the only even prime.

Know the primes up to forty by heart. Two, three, five, seven, eleven, thirteen, seventeen, nineteen, twenty-three, twenty-nine, thirty-one and thirty-seven. And ninety-seven, the largest two-digit prime.

All the other primes are odd. Odd plus odd is even, and odd minus odd is even too. So if two primes give an odd sum or an odd difference, one of them is two. Seventy-three as a sum of two primes? Two plus seventy-one.

To test a number, divide it by the primes up to its square root, and no further. Watch out for the fakes. For three, add the digits, like sixty-nine, six plus nine is fifteen. And never forget to try seven, like seventy-seven, which is seven times eleven.

Every number that isn't prime breaks into primes, in only one way. And it's divisible by every combination of its prime factors. Forty-four is two times two times eleven, so it divides by two, four, eleven, twenty-two and forty-four.
Is a number a divisor? Break it into primes too, and check that every prime is there, enough times. Unpack pieces like six or ten squared first.
Most questions just break a number apart, or build numbers from pieces, and look for the missing prime.
The greatest common divisor takes each shared prime at its lower power. The greatest number that's guaranteed to divide, the LCM, takes every prime at its higher power.

Forty-eight is two to the power of four times three, and sixty is two squared times three times five. The GCD is two squared times three, which is twelve. The LCM takes two to the power of four, three and five, and sixteen times fifteen is two hundred forty.
The trap is just multiplying the two numbers, which counts a shared prime twice. And the GCD times the LCM is the two numbers multiplied.
The number of divisors? Add one to each exponent, and multiply. Two to the power of four times three has five times two, which is ten divisors.
Divisors come in pairs, so only a perfect square has an odd number of them. And exactly three divisors means a prime squared, like four or a hundred twenty-one.
In a perfect square, every exponent is even. Twenty k a square? Twenty is two squared times five, so it needs one more five. k is five, and twenty times five is a hundred, ten squared.

And an equation in primes? Break the number, then match the exponents. Two to the power of a, times three to the power of b, is a hundred forty-four. That's sixteen times nine, which is two to the power of four times three squared, so a is four and b is two.
A prime can't be split between factors, one of them holds it whole.
And when the primes are letters, plug in the smallest primes in the right order, and knock out three choices before you mark one.

Before each question, ask yourself. Did I break every number into primes? Is it really prime, did I try up to the root, and seven? An odd sum or difference, is one of them two? GCD or LCM, lower power or higher power?
The common traps are calling one a prime, forgetting two, and multiplying instead of taking the LCM. [pause] That's it. Now go practice, and I'll see you in the next video.

So we don't know the size of the class, and they ask what it could be. So we don't look for the number itself, we rule out what it can't be. And look at the fractions. There's no such thing as a fifth of a student. [short pause] We'll solve it two ways, step by step with the fractions, and then by building the class from the inside.

[short pause] Let's start step by step. A fifth of the class are basketball boys, and a fifth of a class has to be a whole number of kids. So the class is divisible by five. And remember the sign for five, the last digit is zero or five.
at: So the class is divisible by five

before.say: Thirty-five ends in five, and forty-five ends in five, so they stay. Forty-two and thirty-two don't, so choice numbers three and four are out.

Now the second fraction. A third of the basketball boys play the guitar, so the basketball group has to divide by three. Thirty-five over five is seven basketball boys. A third of seven? Seven doesn't divide by three, so there's no such group. Choice number one is out.
at: the basketball group has to divide

before.say: So forty-five is the only one left, and choice number two is our answer.
at: choice number two is our answer

before: Before you practice, here's a quick summary of division and remainders. Everything important, in a few minutes.

before.say: Two, five and ten, look at the last digit. Three and nine, the digit sum. Four, the last two digits, and eight, the last three.
Eleven, go plus, minus, plus, minus, digit by digit. Nine thirteen, nine minus one plus three is eleven, so it divides by eleven.
A bigger divisor? Split it into parts with no common factor. Thirty-six is four times nine, not six times six.

A number is the divisor times the quotient, plus the remainder, and the remainder is always smaller than the divisor. So the biggest remainder is the divisor minus one. And five divided by eight leaves five, not three.
Dividing by three or nine, the remainder is the same as the digit sum's. Four thousand eight hundred twenty-six, the digit sum is twenty, and twenty divided by nine leaves two.

Only the remainders matter. a leaves five and b leaves seven, dividing by eight. a plus b, five plus seven is twelve, so it leaves four. a times b, five times seven is thirty-five, so it leaves three. a minus b, five minus seven is negative two, so add eight, six.
Take away the remainder, and what's left divides exactly.
A new divisor? It must divide the old one. Leaves eleven by twelve? By four, eleven leaves three. But from ten to four, you can't know.
A fraction of a fraction? Multiply the denominators. How many multiples in a range? The last minus the first, plus one, because both ends count.
Two in a row always divide by two, and three in a row by six. And a cubed minus a is three in a row in disguise.

Necessarily divisible? Tag each condition, and read the number in front. And when you plug in, give different letters different values, avoid values that give zero, and remember that one failing example knocks a choice out.
Before each question, ask yourself. Parts with no common factor? Is my remainder smaller than the divisor? A negative remainder? Add the divisor. And does the new divisor divide the old one?
That's it. Now go practice, and I'll see you in the next video.

changes.bridge: List 66, slide 1 before count-times-middle. Reveal sum=count×average, then average=middle for an odd count of consecutive numbers; retain the existing worked examples and answer 16.

before.say: The sum of seven consecutive integers is ninety-one. What is the largest of them?
So seven numbers in a row, and all we know is their sum. [short pause] We'll solve it two ways, with count times middle, and then with one letter.
at: all we know is their sum

before.say: [short pause] Here's the rule. The sum of numbers in a row is the count times the middle one. Why? The numbers pair up around the middle. One below and one above together are like two middles, so every number counts as the middle.
Let's see it in numbers. Four plus five plus six is fifteen, and that's three times the middle, five. Ten to fourteen, five numbers, add up to sixty, five times the middle, twelve.
So here the middle is the sum over the count, ninety-one over seven, thirteen. That's the fourth number, with three below it and three above it, ten up to sixteen.
The largest is sixteen, so choice number three is our answer.
at: choice number three is our answer

before.say: Now careful, thirteen is the trap. It's the middle, not the largest.
[pause] Another way is one letter, around the middle, b. The seven numbers are b minus three up to b plus three. The minuses and the pluses cancel, so the sum is seven b.
Seven b is ninety-one, so b is ninety-one over seven, thirteen. And the largest is b plus three, sixteen. Choice number three. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.

after.say: The sum of seven consecutive integers is ninety-one. What is the largest of them?
So seven numbers in a row, and all we know is their sum. [short pause] We'll solve it two ways, with count times middle, and then with one letter.
at: all we know is their sum

after.say: Remember what we learned in averages. The average is the sum divided by the number of values. So the sum is the number of values times their average. Here we have seven numbers, so their sum is seven times their average.

And why is the average the middle number here? The numbers are consecutive, so the gaps are equal. The number one below the middle pairs with the number one above it. Together they make twice the middle. The same happens two below and two above, and three below and three above. So the average is the middle number, and we can use count times middle.
at: So the average is the middle

after.say: Here's the rule for an odd count of consecutive integers. The sum is the count times the middle number. Seven is an odd count, so there is one actual middle number, the fourth.
Let's see it in numbers. Four plus five plus six is fifteen, and that's three times the middle, five. Ten to fourteen, five numbers, add up to sixty, five times the middle, twelve.

before.say: Remember, an even number is an integer that divides by two, like five seventy-two, or nine thousand one fifty, and zero is even too. An odd number is an integer that isn't even.

And remember adding. Even plus even is even, eight plus twelve is twenty. Odd plus odd is even, seven plus eleven is eighteen. Even plus odd is odd, eight plus seven is fifteen. Subtracting works the same.

So in a long sum, the even numbers don't matter at all, and only the odd ones count. Eight plus five minus two plus eleven plus three. The odd ones are five, eleven and three, three of them. Two of them pair up into an even, and one is left over, so the total is odd. And really, it's twenty-five.
Four plus seven minus ten plus nine. Only two odd ones, seven and nine, and they pair up, so the total is even. It's ten.
Multiplying. One even factor is enough to make the whole product even, because it brings a two in. Four times fifteen is sixty, and nine times eight is seventy-two.
So a product is odd only when every factor is odd. Seven times three is twenty-one, odd.
Careful with brackets. Two times, in brackets, x plus seven, is even, because the two multiplies everything. But two x plus seven is odd. With x one, the first is sixteen, and the second is nine.
Dividing is different, because you can almost always get a fraction. Odd over odd is odd, or a fraction. Twenty-one over seven is three, and seven over three is a fraction.
Even over odd is even, or a fraction. Twelve over three is four, and eight over three is a fraction.
Odd over even is always a fraction. Seven over two, nine over four. Why? An even number has a two inside, and an odd number has no two to cancel it.

Powers don't change parity. Two squared is four, two cubed is eight, even. Three squared is nine, three cubed is twenty-seven, odd. A power just multiplies the same number again and again. So in a parity question, you may drop the powers.

before.say: A and B represent digits. Given: two A six, plus B eight, is equal to three A four. B is equal to what?
Two numbers with a letter in the middle. [short pause] We'll solve it two ways, with the columns, and then with the algebraic form.
[short pause] Let's start with the columns. The ones, six plus eight is fourteen. Write four, it matches, and carry one.

The tens, A plus B plus the one ends in A. Now careful, a lot of students say ends in A, so B is zero. But there's a carry. A plus zero plus one ends in A plus one, not A. So choice number two is the trap.

at: B plus one has to be ten

before.say: With any A. Take five, two fifty-six plus ninety-eight is three fifty-four. So in a middle column, ends in the same digit means zero or nine, depending on the carry. And a carry from two numbers is at most one. Three or four numbers can carry two or three.

before.say: Ten A is on both sides, it cancels, and that's why A can be any digit. Ten B is three hundred four minus two hundred fourteen, which is ninety. So B is nine. Choice number four. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.

before: Before you practice, here's a quick summary of the topic. What the letters mean, the four steps, and the number facts.

before.say: A bar on top means the letters are the digits of one number. A B is ten A plus B, not A times B. And A B C is a hundred A, plus ten B, plus C.
The same letter is always the same digit, and a leading digit is never zero. Different letters? Only if the question says so.
Write it vertically, check the units digit, check the leftmost digit and the size, and then plug in. One letter asked? Plug in the choices.

A puzzle in words, with no columns? Write the number as ten A plus B, and collect the letters on each side. Ten A plus B equals three times A plus B gives seven A equals two B, so the number is twenty-seven.
In the ones column nothing carries in, so X plus Y ends in X means Y is zero. In any other column there may be a carry, so it's zero or nine.
Two numbers, and the sum has more digits? The leading digit is one. Seventy-six plus fifty-eight is one thirty-four. Only for two numbers.
The special digits, zero, one, five and six, keep their units digit when multiplied by themselves. Fifteen times fifteen is two twenty-five, and sixteen times sixteen is two fifty-six.
A subtraction? Flip it into an addition. A division? Flip it into a multiplication.
A number plus its reversal divides by eleven, minus its reversal by nine, and with three digits, by ninety-nine.
A A A is a hundred eleven times A, so it divides by three and by thirty-seven. Four forty-four is thirty-seven times twelve.
at: A A A is a hundred eleven
